hints: Think about what is different between the input $V_{IN}$ in Fig. 6.1 and the output $V_{OUT}$ - one changes direction regularly, the other flows one way only.
walkthrough:
**What a.c. and d.c. mean**
You already know that in a.c. the current reverses direction every half cycle, so $V_{IN}$ goes positive then negative. In d.c. the current is always in the same direction, so the voltage stays on one side of zero.

**Link to the circuit**
The box in Fig. 6.1 takes the alternating $V_{IN}$ and forces the output to stay positive. That process of making current unidirectional is rectification.
Final answer: Rectification is the conversion of alternating current (a.c.) to direct current (d.c.).

hints: Look at Fig. 6.2 - the rectified output without a capacitor would fall to zero between peaks, but $V_{OUT}$ stays high near 8 to 12 V. What does the capacitor do when the voltage tries to fall?
walkthrough:
**Why smoothing is needed**
Rectification alone still gives large pulses that drop to zero. Most electronic devices need a steadier d.c. voltage, so we need to fill in the gaps.

**How the capacitor helps**
When the rectified voltage rises, C charges up. When the rectified voltage falls, C cannot discharge back through the rectifier, so it discharges slowly through R, keeping $V_{OUT}$ high. This is called smoothing.
Final answer: Capacitor C smooths the rectified output, storing charge when $V_{OUT}$ is high and discharging through R to maintain $V_{OUT}$ when the rectified voltage falls.

hints: Look at the dashed $V_{IN}$ curve in Fig. 6.2. What is its maximum value at $t = 0$, and what is the time for one complete oscillation back to the same point?
Recall how the peak value relates to $A$ in $A \cos Bt$, and how the repeat time $T$ relates to $B$ through $B = 2\pi / T$. Check units are ms on the graph.
walkthrough:
**Find the amplitude A**
At $t = 0$, $\cos Bt = 1$, so $V_{IN} = A$. From Fig. 6.2 the dashed curve starts at $12 \text{ V}$. So $$A = 12 \text{ V}$$

**Find the period T**
The dashed $V_{IN}$ curve repeats after one full cosine cycle. It peaks at $t = 0$, goes negative, and returns to $+12 \text{ V}$ at $t = 20 \text{ ms}$. So $$T = 20 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$$

**Convert period to B**
For a cosine wave, $$B = \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ $$B = \frac{2\pi}{20 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 3.1 \times 10^{2} \text{ rad s}^{-1}$$
Final answer: $A = 12 \text{ V}$, $B = 3.1 \times 10^{2} \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

hints: Count how many $V_{OUT}$ peaks occur for one $V_{IN}$ cycle in Fig. 6.2 - does the output use both the positive and negative halves of the input?
walkthrough:
**Compare input and output frequencies**
$V_{IN}$ has period $20 \text{ ms}$, but $V_{OUT}$ peaks every $10 \text{ ms}$ at $t = 10, 20, 30, 40 \text{ ms}$. Both halves of the a.c. cycle are being turned into positive output.

**Name the type**
Using both halves is full-wave rectification. Half-wave would give only one peak per $20 \text{ ms}$ and $V_{OUT}$ would fall to zero in between.
Final answer: Full-wave rectification.

hints: Remember that full-wave rectification needs to steer current so that Y is always positive relative to Z, whichever way W and X are. How many one-way paths (diodes) are needed to do this?
Think of a diamond shape: the a.c. input W, X go to opposite corners, and the d.c. output Y, Z come from the other two corners, with all diodes pointing toward Y and away from Z.
walkthrough:
**Why four diodes**
A single diode gives half-wave. To invert the negative half-cycle you need a bridge of four diodes that automatically routes current the same way through the load.

**How to connect them**
Join W to Y and to Z via two diodes in opposite senses, and join X to Y and to Z via two diodes in opposite senses, forming a diamond. Arrange all diode arrows so conventional current always flows into Y and out of Z. For example, W to Y forward, X to Y forward, Z to W forward, Z to X forward. This ensures Y is always positive with respect to Z.
Final answer: Four diodes connected as a bridge rectifier between W, X (a.c. input) and Y, Z (d.c. output), with diodes conducting toward Y and away from Z.

hints: Focus on one falling section of $V_{OUT}$ in Fig. 6.2, e.g. from the 12 V peak down to about 8.0 V just before the next rise. This fall is the capacitor discharging through R.
Read off from the graph the starting voltage $V_{0}$, the finishing voltage $V$, and the time $t$ taken for that fall. Remember $t$ is in ms.
Think about which mathematical law links $V$, $V_{0}$, $t$ and the time constant $\tau$ for exponential discharge, and how you can rearrange it to find $\tau$.
walkthrough:
**Identify the discharge**
Between peaks, the rectifier supplies no current, so C discharges through R. Voltage follows $$V = V_{0} e^{-t/\tau}$$ where $\tau = RC$ and $t$ is time since the peak.

**Read values from Fig. 6.2**
Take $V_{0} = 12 \text{ V}$ at a peak, e.g. $t = 10 \text{ ms}$. The voltage falls to $V = 8.0 \text{ V}$ just before the next peak. The time interval is $$t \approx 7.3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$$

**Solve for the time constant**
Substitute: $$8.0 = 12 \exp\left(\frac{-7.3 \times 10^{-3}}{\tau}\right)$$ $$\frac{8.0}{12} = \exp\left(\frac{-7.3 \times 10^{-3}}{\tau}\right)$$ Take natural log: $$\ln(0.667) = \frac{-7.3 \times 10^{-3}}{\tau}$$ $$\tau = \frac{-7.3 \times 10^{-3}}{-0.405} \approx 1.8 \times 10^{-2} \text{ s}$$
Final answer: $\tau \approx 1.8 \times 10^{-2} \text{ s}$ (0.018 s)

hints: Recall what physical quantities multiply together to give the time constant for a capacitor discharging through a resistor.
You know $\tau$ from (b)(iv) and $C = 570 \mu\text{F}$. Check the micro prefix conversion before rearranging to find $R$.
walkthrough:
**Use the time constant relation**
For discharge through a resistor, $$\tau = RC$$ So $$R = \frac{\tau}{C}$$

**Substitute numbers**
With $\tau = 0.018 \text{ s}$ and $C = 570 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F}$: $$R = \frac{0.018}{570 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 32 \text{ } \Omega$$ A larger R would give slower discharge and less ripple.
Final answer: $R \approx 32 \text{ } \Omega$
